subject: Endocrine
vignette: A 36-year-old woman has 6 months of fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, and weight gain. Examination shows a moderately enlarged, nontender thyroid gland. TSH is 22 µIU/mL with a low free T4, and antibodies against thyroid peroxidase and thyroglobulin are elevated. She recalls a brief episode of palpitations and weight loss 8 months ago that resolved spontaneously.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Hashimoto thyroiditis
Subacute granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis
Riedel thyroiditis
Graves disease
Postpartum thyroiditis

explanation_correct: Hashimoto thyroiditis (chronic autoimmune thyroiditis) is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient regions. It produces a moderately enlarged, nontender thyroid with anti-thyroid peroxidase (antimicrosomal) and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies, Hürthle cells, and lymphoid aggregates with germinal centers. A transient preceding hyperthyroid state called Hashitoxicosis can occur from follicular rupture and hormone release, matching her earlier episode. It is associated with HLA-DR3 and an increased risk of primary thyroid lymphoma.

explanation_incorrect.B: De Quervain thyroiditis is typically a very tender, post-viral gland with elevated ESR and granulomatous inflammation, not a nontender gland with anti-TPO antibodies.
explanation_incorrect.C: Riedel thyroiditis produces a hard, rocklike, fixed nontender gland from dense fibrosis, often within IgG4-related disease, rather than autoimmune serologies.
explanation_incorrect.D: Graves disease causes hyperthyroidism with suppressed TSH, diffuse goiter, and ophthalmopathy, the opposite of this hypothyroid laboratory pattern.
explanation_incorrect.E: Postpartum thyroiditis arises within 1 year of delivery and is self-limited; no recent delivery is described here.

educationalObjective: Hashimoto thyroiditis is the leading cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient regions, with a nontender goiter, anti-TPO antibodies, Hürthle cells, and possible preceding Hashitoxicosis.

subject: Endocrine
vignette: A 58-year-old woman with long-standing Hashimoto thyroiditis, HLA-DR3 positivity, and Hürthle cells on a prior biopsy presents with rapid enlargement of one thyroid lobe, hoarseness, and cervical lymphadenopathy over 3 months. The gland is nontender and she has no fever. Her TSH remains elevated.
question: Which malignancy is she at increased risk of developing?

options.text: Medullary thyroid carcinoma
Papillary thyroid carcinoma with psammoma bodies
Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma
Primary thyroid diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
Follicular thyroid carcinoma with capsular invasion

explanation_correct: Hashimoto thyroiditis carries an increased risk of primary thyroid lymphoma, most often diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. The background of chronic autoimmune lymphocytic infiltration with lymphoid aggregates and germinal centers is the presumed substrate. Rapid enlargement of a previously stable Hashimoto gland with hoarseness or nodal disease should raise suspicion for this complication. Hashimoto is also associated with HLA-DR3 and is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient regions.

explanation_incorrect.A: Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells and is linked to RET mutations and MEN2, not Hashimoto thyroiditis.
explanation_incorrect.B: Papillary thyroid carcinoma with psammoma bodies is the most common thyroid cancer overall but is not the classic Hashimoto-associated malignancy.
explanation_incorrect.C: Anaplastic carcinoma is a highly aggressive tumor; the fibrotic, invasive mimic in this setting is Riedel thyroiditis, while Hashimoto predisposes to lymphoma.
explanation_incorrect.E: Follicular carcinoma with capsular invasion is not the tumor classically associated with chronic autoimmune thyroiditis.

educationalObjective: Hashimoto thyroiditis increases the risk of primary thyroid lymphoma, typically diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.

subject: Endocrine
vignette: A 29-year-old woman gave birth 8 weeks ago. For 6 weeks she had palpitations, heat intolerance, and weight loss with a suppressed TSH, followed by fatigue, cold intolerance, and an elevated TSH. Her thyroid is small and nontender; she has no fever and no thyroid pain. She had a similar mild, self-limited episode after her first delivery.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this disorder?

options.text: Self-limited granulomatous inflammation with elevated ESR and a very tender thyroid
A mild self-limited variant of Hashimoto thyroiditis with hyperthyroidism within 3 months followed by hypothyroidism and recovery
Progressive autoimmune destruction requiring lifelong levothyroxine in most affected women
IgG4-related fibrosis that extends to the trachea and esophagus
Iodine excess causing Wolff-Chaikoff inhibition of thyroid hormone synthesis

explanation_correct: Postpartum thyroiditis is a mild, self-limited variant of Hashimoto thyroiditis that arises within 1 year after delivery. Its natural history is hyperthyroidism within 3 months of birth, followed by a hypothyroid phase, and then recovery to a euthyroid state. The gland is typically nontender and there is no granulomatous inflammation or elevated ESR. Recognition is important because the condition usually resolves and does not imply permanent hypothyroidism.

explanation_incorrect.A: Painful thyroid tenderness, elevated ESR, and granulomatous inflammation describe subacute de Quervain thyroiditis, not postpartum thyroiditis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Postpartum thyroiditis is self-limited with recovery to euthyroidism in most patients, rather than progressive destruction needing lifelong replacement.
explanation_incorrect.D: IgG4-related fibrosis with tracheal or esophageal extension describes Riedel invasive fibrous thyroiditis.
explanation_incorrect.E: The Wolff-Chaikoff effect is inhibition of hormone synthesis by excess iodine and does not produce this postpartum triphasic course.

educationalObjective: Postpartum thyroiditis is a self-limited Hashimoto variant occurring within a year of delivery, with hyperthyroidism within 3 months, then hypothyroidism, then recovery.

subject: Endocrine
vignette: A 44-year-old woman develops severe anterior neck pain radiating to the jaw 3 weeks after an upper respiratory infection. She has palpitations and heat intolerance. TSH is suppressed and free T4 is elevated; ESR is 62 mm/hr. The thyroid is exquisitely tender to palpation. Over the next 2 months she becomes hypothyroid before eventually recovering euthyroidism.
question: Which of the following best identifies the underlying pathologic process?

options.text: Autoantibody-mediated follicular destruction with Hürthle cells and lymphoid germinal centers
IgG4-positive plasma cell infiltration replacing the gland with dense fibrosis
TSH receptor stimulation by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin
Retroorbital lymphocytic infiltration with hydrophilic GAG secretion
Self-limited granulomatous inflammation after a viral infection with transient hormone release from follicular disruption

explanation_correct: Subacute granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis is usually a self-limited, often post-viral illness characterized by a very tender thyroid, jaw pain, and elevated ESR with granulomatous inflammation. Follicular disruption releases preformed hormone, causing transient hyperthyroidism with suppressed TSH, followed by a euthyroid phase, a hypothyroid phase, and finally recovery. The striking tenderness, viral prodrome, and triphasic course distinguish it from Hashimoto and Graves disease. Pain control and, if needed, glucocorticoids are used for symptom relief.

explanation_incorrect.A: Hürthle cells, lymphoid germinal centers, and anti-TPO antibodies define Hashimoto thyroiditis, which is typically nontender and lacks the post-viral triphasic course.
explanation_incorrect.B: Dense IgG4-related fibrosis with a hard fixed gland characterizes Riedel thyroiditis, not a tender self-limited post-viral thyroiditis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin causing diffuse goiter and hyperthyroidism is Graves disease, which is not tender, post-viral, or associated with a high ESR.
explanation_incorrect.D: Retroorbital GAG deposition is the mechanism of Graves ophthalmopathy and does not explain a painful thyroid.

educationalObjective: Subacute granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis is a painful, self-limited post-viral illness with high ESR and a transient hyperthyroid, then hypothyroid, then euthyroid course.

subject: Endocrine
vignette: A 61-year-old man has a slowly enlarging, rock-hard, fixed, nontender thyroid gland. He also has a history of autoimmune pancreatitis and retroperitoneal fibrosis. TSH is elevated with a low free T4. CT shows fibrotic tissue extending toward the trachea and esophagus, prompting concern for an invasive malignancy.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma with direct local invasion
Hashimoto thyroiditis with a fibrous variant
Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis
Riedel (invasive fibrous) thyroiditis as part of IgG4-related disease
Medullary thyroid carcinoma with desmoplastic stroma

explanation_correct: Riedel thyroiditis (invasive fibrous thyroiditis) may occur as part of the IgG4-related disease spectrum, which also includes autoimmune pancreatitis, retroperitoneal fibrosis, and noninfectious aortitis. It produces a slowly enlarging, hard, rocklike, fixed, nontender thyroid because the gland is replaced by fibrous tissue and an inflammatory infiltrate. Fibrosis can extend to the trachea and esophagus, mimicking anaplastic carcinoma, and about one-third of patients are hypothyroid. The systemic IgG4 associations and nontender hard gland are the discriminating features.

explanation_incorrect.A: Anaplastic carcinoma is aggressively destructive rather than slowly enlarging and lacks the IgG4-related systemic fibrosis seen here; Riedel thyroiditis mimics it.
explanation_incorrect.B: Hashimoto thyroiditis gives a moderately enlarged nontender gland with anti-TPO antibodies and lymphoid aggregates, not a rock-hard fixed gland with systemic fibrosis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis is very tender, follows a viral illness, has an elevated ESR, and resolves spontaneously.
explanation_incorrect.E: Medullary thyroid carcinoma is linked to RET/MEN2 and calcitonin production and does not produce IgG4-related retroperitoneal fibrosis.

educationalObjective: Riedel thyroiditis is an IgG4-related fibrotic disease causing a hard, fixed, nontender gland that mimics anaplastic carcinoma and causes hypothyroidism in about one-third of patients.

subject: Endocrine
vignette: Newborn screening shows a markedly elevated TSH and low free T4 in a 2-week-old infant. Examination reveals a pale, puffy-faced child with a pot-bellied abdomen, a protruding umbilicus, and a large protuberant tongue. The mother had an uncomplicated pregnancy in an iodine-sufficient region, and the infant has no goiter.
question: Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this condition?

options.text: Thyroid dysgenesis such as agenesis, hypoplasia, or ectopy
Maternal iodine deficiency
Autoimmune Hashimoto thyroiditis with anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies
Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis after a viral infection
Iodine excess producing a Wolff-Chaikoff effect

explanation_correct: Congenital hypothyroidism, formerly called cretinism, is most commonly caused by thyroid dysgenesis (agenesis, hypoplasia, or ectopy) or dyshormonogenesis in iodine-sufficient regions. Affected infants show the 6 P's: pot-bellied, pale, puffy-faced, protruding umbilicus, protuberant tongue, and poor brain development. Untreated disease causes irreversible intellectual disability, which is why newborn screening is essential. The absence of a goiter and the iodine-sufficient setting argue against iodine deficiency.

explanation_incorrect.B: Iodine deficiency is the most common cause of hypothyroidism worldwide and typically produces a goiter, but the mother lives in an iodine-sufficient region and the infant has no goiter.
explanation_incorrect.C: Hashimoto thyroiditis can cause congenital hypothyroidism but dysgenesis is more common in iodine-sufficient regions; autoantibodies are not mentioned here.
explanation_incorrect.D: Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis is a painful post-viral illness, not a cause of congenital hypothyroidism in a newborn.
explanation_incorrect.E: Iodine excess causing Wolff-Chaikoff inhibition is not the typical mechanism of congenital hypothyroidism and would not explain the dysmorphic 6 P's phenotype.

educationalObjective: Congenital hypothyroidism is most often due to thyroid dysgenesis in iodine-sufficient regions and presents with the 6 P's, including poor brain development.

subject: Endocrine
vignette: A 68-year-old man is critically ill in the intensive care unit with sepsis and multiorgan failure. Thyroid testing shows a markedly decreased total T3, a normal-to-low free T4, and a TSH that is not elevated. He has no goiter or thyroid tenderness and no prior thyroid disease. He is not hypothermic or bradycardic.
question: Which of the following best explains these thyroid function tests?

options.text: Primary hypothyroidism due to Hashimoto thyroiditis
Nonthyroidal illness syndrome (euthyroid sick syndrome) with decreased T3
Secondary hyperthyroidism from a TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma
Subacute thyroiditis during its transient hyperthyroid phase
Graves disease with suppressed TSH and elevated free T4

explanation_correct: Nonthyroidal illness syndrome (euthyroid sick syndrome) occurs in critically ill patients and is characterized by decreased T3 with normal or decreased T4 and TSH. It reflects altered peripheral conversion and binding during severe illness rather than intrinsic thyroid disease, so it generally is not treated with thyroid hormone. Other causes of hypothyroidism to distinguish include iodine deficiency (most common worldwide, with goiter), iodine excess (Wolff-Chaikoff effect), and drugs such as amiodarone and lithium. Hashimoto thyroiditis, by contrast, would show an elevated TSH and a low free T4 with anti-TPO antibodies.

explanation_incorrect.A: Hashimoto thyroiditis would produce an elevated TSH and low free T4 with anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies, not isolated low T3 with a non-elevated TSH in critical illness.
explanation_incorrect.C: A TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma would raise both TSH and free T4, producing biochemical hyperthyroidism rather than low T3.
explanation_incorrect.D: Subacute thyroiditis causes a tender gland, elevated ESR, and transient high free T4 with suppressed TSH, not the pattern seen in this septic patient.
explanation_incorrect.E: Graves disease shows elevated free T4 and T3 with suppressed TSH and thyrotoxic symptoms, the opposite of these results.

educationalObjective: Nonthyroidal illness syndrome in critically ill patients shows low T3 with normal or low T4 and TSH and must be distinguished from true hypothyroidism and other causes such as iodine excess or drugs.
